newsitem.title: ROMANIA: IMF warns Romania on risks of shying from reform.
newsitem.headline: IMF warns Romania on risks of shying from reform.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund has warned Romania that failure to carry out structural reform risks ending the country's fragile economic recovery.

In its annual report, the IMF chastised the Balkan country for failing to liberalise its foreign exchange market, as agreed, and pinpointed costly loss-making state businesses as the greatest obstacle to future growth.
"It was most important that forceful action be taken to reform problem enterprises in state-owned industry and agriculture," said the annual report released on Thursday in Washington.

The IMF's comments were in line with the position it adopted earlier this year when it withheld loan tranches after Romania restricted the forex market to keep the local leu currency high and beat inflation before November elections.
Under a standby agreement due to expire in April 1997, the IMF had offered Romania some $280 million in loans.

Romania is now looking elsewhere for funds, with a $150 million syndicated loan subscription due to close on Monday and a 30 billion yen samurai bond issue expected next week, on top of previous bond raisings.
But the IMF report makes clear it thinks international capital market financing will become more difficult unless Romania heeds its advice.

"The authorities (must) avoid further policy slippages or reversals...otherwise they risked undermining confidence in the economy, jeopardizing the economic recovery and posing a risk to the country's external postion," the report said.
It called for tough measures to rein in budget deficits and wage increases, hasten privatisation and slush subsidies to bloated communist-era industrial enterprises.

Analysts said the ruling leftist Party of Social Democracy of President Ion Iliescu, in power since the 1989 fall of communism, has shied from reform for fear of alienating its working class supporters by shutting loss-making factories.

Chief economist at the Romanian National Bank, Dan Daianu, said last week a post-election macro-stabilisation package was essential, but analysts question the degree of political will that exists to take such tough measures.
